ground_truth: The Commission conducted extensive stakeholder consultations. ground_truth: According to Article 43(1), for high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III point 1 (which covers biometric identification), if the provider has not applied harmonised standards referred to in Article 40 (or applied them only in part), and common specifications under Article 41 are not available, the provider must follow the conformity assessment procedure set out in Annex VII. ground_truth: According to Article 28(1)(b), if a distributor modifies the intended purpose of a high-risk AI system already placed on the market, they shall be considered a provider for the purposes of this Regulation and become subject to all obligations of the provider under Article 16. This includes ensuring compliance with Chapter 2 requirements, having a quality management system (Article 17), drawing up technical documentation, undergoing conformity assessment (Article 19), drawing up an EU declaration of conformity (Article 48), affixing CE marking (Article 49), and registering in the EU database (Article 51). Per Article 28(2), the original provider is no longer considered the provider once this occurs.

Key insights include:  1. **Penalty Frameworks for Private Companies**:    - **Tiered Fines**: Private companies face administrative fines of up to €30M or 6% of global turnover for severe violations (e.g., prohibited AI practices or non-compliance with system requirements). For other violations, fines range up to €20M or 4% of turnover, and up to €10M or 2% for misleading information.    - **Enforcement**: Penalties are enforced by **Member State authorities** under national rules, with oversight from the European AI Board for consistency.  2. **Penalty Frameworks for EU Institutions**:    - **EDPS Oversight**: The **European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS)** imposes fines on EU institutions, agencies, and bodies. ground_truth: For private companies, Member States lay down penalty rules (Article 71(1)), with three tiers: up to €30M or 6% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices (Article 5) and data requirements (Article 10) violations; up to €20M or 4% for other non-compliance; up to €10M or 2% for misleading information. For EU institutions, agencies and bodies, the European Data Protection Supervisor (not Member States) imposes fines (Article 72). The fines are significantly lower: up to €500,000 for violations of Article 5 and Article 10; up to €250,000 for other non-compliance. The EDPS considers similar factors (nature, gravity, duration, cooperation, previous infringements) but the maximum amounts are drastically reduced compared to the private sector framework.

The market surveillance authority acts under Article 65 when such risks are identified.  2. **Actions Under Article 65**: The authority may impose corrective measures (e.g., recalls, bans) or refer the case to the European AI Board for Union-wide coordination.  3. **Union Safeguard Procedure**: This procedure is initiated when a risk is deemed cross-border. ground_truth: Under Article 65, when a market surveillance authority finds an AI system presents a risk, it evaluates compliance and can require corrective actions, withdrawal, or recall. The provider must take these actions across all Member States within a prescribed timeline (Article 65(4)). The authority notifies the Commission and other Member States (Article 65(5)). Under the Union safeguard procedure (Article 66), if within three months another Member State objects or the Commission considers the measure contrary to Union law, the Commission evaluates the national measure and decides within 9 months whether it is justified. If justified, all Member States must withdraw the non-compliant AI system from their markets (Article 66(2)). If the non-compliance is attributed to shortcomings in harmonised standards, the Commission may initiate the procedure under Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 1025/2012 (Article 66(3)).

ground_truth: Article 13 applies specifically to high-risk AI systems (Title III) and requires operational transparency enabling users to interpret outputs appropriately, plus detailed instructions for use including: provider identity, performance characteristics/limitations, intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity metrics, human oversight measures, expected lifetime, and maintenance instructions. Article 52 applies to certain AI systems regardless of risk level (Title IV) and addresses three specific scenarios: (1) AI systems interacting with natural persons must inform people they are interacting with AI; (2) emotion recognition/biometric categorisation systems must inform exposed persons; (3) deepfake content must be disclosed as artificially generated. Both have exceptions for law enforcement. Article 13 is about enabling informed use by professional users, while Article 52 protects general public awareness of AI interaction.

ground_truth: Article 17 requires providers to put a quality management system (QMS) in place covering regulatory compliance strategy, design procedures, development quality control, testing procedures, technical specifications, data management, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, communication handling, record keeping, and resource management. The conformity assessment under Article 43 has two routes: Annex VI (internal control, where the provider self-assesses including QMS compliance) and Annex VII (involving a notified body). Under Annex VII, the notified body (which must satisfy organizational and independence requirements per Article 33) assesses both the QMS and the technical documentation. The notified body verifies that the QMS ensures compliance (linking back to Article 17's requirements). For credit institutions under Directive 2013/36/EU, the QMS obligation is deemed fulfilled by complying with internal governance rules under Article 74 of that Directive (Article 17(3)).

ground_truth: A small-scale provider (micro or small enterprise per Recommendation 2003/361/EC, Article 3(3)) benefits from several support measures: priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes (Article 55(1)(a)), which provide a controlled environment for development, testing, and validation under authority supervision (Article 53(1)). They receive specific awareness-raising activities (Article 55(1)(b)), dedicated communication channels for guidance (Article 55(1)(c)), and reduced conformity assessment fees proportionate to their size (Article 55(2)).
